In a sense that she is very willing to speak, but she regularly drowns the students in unnecessary detail. Rather than painting a clear picture, she usually projects her inner thoughts over strange details on unnecessary parts of the subject. This carries on to such an extent that it is more than common for her to extend her class into break time, usually around 4-8 minutes of that 10 minute break. This could also be because of her not reaching the desired point of the lecture for that day BECAUSE SHE IS TOO BUSY TALKING ABOUT UNNECESSARY DETAILS DURING SAID CLASS-TIME. (terrible time management) As a person who isn't planning to study "Architectural History" professionally, it is safe to say that being drowned in said details is less than enjoyable. This is the case for many other students in my class who aren't very interested in the course and this leads to my second issue: Miss Semra takes this VERY personally. She usually portrays negative behavior towards this lack of participation, in a sense that she personally gets angry or desperate or sad, effecting the quality of the lecture. course: ADA264 is a boring but logical course. It is quite straightforward and could be easy or hard based on two factors: The teaching quality of the instructor and the difficulty of the exams. For this semester, I would argue that the exams were too difficult and unfair for the student. The questions primarily were based on memorization and after that, analytical thinking. So without both traits, It was impossible to answer the questions completely. All of the questions were the same format so there were no specific "easy" or "difficult" questions. In my opinion, this leads to an exam being more luck based, rather than selective. By creating specific difficulty thresholds, it is quite easy to separate students. Other than this, I would argue that this course is way too difficult and time consuming for the amount of hours it has (3). It would be a better idea to reduce the memorization and increase the amount of analytical thinking required to pass this course. Perhaps than, it would be a greater idea to introduce another course of history which now gets into greater memory-based detail as an elective course for the interested students who would like to pursue Architectural History.
